title: Subcutaneous injection
what: Medicine is given with a thin, short needle into the fat layer under the skin, usually on the belly, upper arm, or thigh.
why: This is how insulin, blood clot medicines, some hormones, and vaccines are given, as your doctor prescribes.
duration: the injection itself takes less than a minute
tell_doctor: If you had bruises or lumps after injections before

prepare.title: Prep
prepare.text: Usually none. You can eat and drink.

prepare.title: Clothing
prepare.text: Clothes that make it easy to uncover your belly or upper arm.

bring: The medicine, if you bought it yourself
steps: The nurse checks the prescription and the medicine
A spot is chosen: the belly around the navel, the upper arm, or the thigh
The skin is wiped with antiseptic
The skin is pinched into a fold, and the needle goes in quickly
The medicine is given slowly, and the needle comes out
feel: Some medicines sting a little as they go in
after: Do not rub the spot, unless the nurse says otherwise
A small bruise can happen and goes away on its own
For a course of injections, use a different spot each time
red_flags: Swelling of the face or lips, trouble breathing, or a rash all over: call emergency services
The injection site becomes very red, hot, and painful

faq.a: There is plenty of fat under the skin there, so the medicine is absorbed evenly. It does not hurt more than the arm.

faq.q: Why do I get bruises after belly injections?
faq.a: Blood clot medicines often cause bruises. If they are very large, tell your doctor.

reminders.text: Injection soon. Wear clothes that make it easy to uncover your belly or upper arm.
